about: Independent verdict (0017) on the #218/#226 change (docs/decisions/0059) to the tax map: method-of-allocation declares definedElsewhere beside its ambiguity block, drops the crossReferences item that stood in for it, and returns MissingRulesData. The reviewer was a separate agent context given only: the corpus text of 26 CFR 1.121-1; a before/after of the one changed entry; four sibling entries; the manifest's references; the correspondence table and the definedElsewhere specification; and 0026. It was told not to read the repository, the issues, or any decision record above 0026. `sha256` is the final map. `rounds` keeps both rounds unedited.
summary: Round 1: 3 agree, 3 disagree, against a broken diff the reviewer caught. Round 2 on the real transition: 4 agree, 2 disagree.
aFaultInTheReview: Round 1's diff.json was cut against a commit that already held the change, so `before` and `after` were the same object. The reviewer found that itself and said so before answering. Three of its six questions could not be judged and its `semanticallyInert: true` was withdrawn in round 2 as false against the real diff. Recorded because a verdict's worth depends on what it was shown, and this one was shown the wrong thing once.
whatTheReviewChanged: Round 1 found, and the corpus confirms, that the entry's `ambiguity.question` names '(e)(4) Example 6' as the case where no method exists and is wrong about it: Example 6 is use within the dwelling unit, where (e)(1) requires no allocation and (e)(3) never fires. Filed as #407 rather than corrected here. Round 2 then held that filing it was not enough, because the change's own appended text rested on the same gap: the note now states the gap without the example, names #407, and says the gap stands on the face of (e)(3). Round 2 also asked for three things the note now carries: that the deleted item's claim about the schema was true when written and 0059 is what makes it false; that the item was the only reference to finding 4 of the trial report; and that admitting section 1250(b)(3) would oblige splitting this entry, because row 3 would stop answering and row 6 would answer wrongly for the depreciation-taken branch. Two round-1 objections it withdrew on its own reading: that row 2 swallows every mapped entry (the table marks it a pipeline gate), and that one reason cannot serve both branches (a caller cannot establish which branch they are in without the statute).

openAfterTwoRounds.finding: `ambiguity.question` and the note name Example 6 as the gap case and it is not one.

The interpretive gap is no longer machine-readable: `unresolvedReason` records the runtime row, and only prose says an interpretation is missing. Recorded as a cost in 0059 rather than answered with a field 0005 would refuse.

The entry does not name `dwelling-unit-definition` in `dependsOn`, reaching the term only transitively, and that entry's note claims three dependants where one is visible. Outside the material the reviewer was given.
openAfterTwoRounds.filedAs: not filed; needs counting against the whole map

openAfterTwoRounds.finding: Four phrasings of the depreciation predicate are in play -- 'no depreciation was ever taken', 'is not entitled to claim', 'depreciation adjustments attributable to the property', and the note's 'where no depreciation was taken' -- and which governs is settleable only from section 1250(b)(3).

hardActionItem: Round 2 asked for one thing to be run rather than argued: check-map.py against the changed map, to confirm an `ambiguity` block beside `definedElsewhere` is accepted. It is -- `--only exclusions` reports 1 ok, 0 failed, and the whole map reports 21 ok, 0 failed. So the deleted item's claim was true when written and 0059 is what changed it, which is now said in the entry's own note.

preliminary.finding: The diff I was given is not the change described in the brief. diff.json's before and after are the SAME JSON object: they differ only in the position of the definedElsewhere key (after ambiguity vs. after enabledBy). The brief says the before carried a crossReferences item with an unmapped reason and unresolvedReason RequiresInterpretation. Neither is in the before. The before already carries definedElsewhere usc-26-1250, already says MissingRulesData, has no crossReferences at all, and its note is byte-identical to the after's. Verified: json.load(before) == json.load(after) is True. So either diff.json was cut against an already-changed file, or the brief describes a different revision. Everything below judges the entry as it stands in both halves; the judgement on questions 1-3 and 6 is about the entry, not about a change, because there is no change in this file.

verdicts.citation: using the same method of allocation that the taxpayer used to determine depreciation adjustments (as defined in section 1250(b)(3)), if applicable.
verdicts.reason: definedElsewhere is defensible, but only just, and for a narrower reason than the entry gives. The rule's OUTPUT -- the method the taxpayer actually used -- is a caller-supplied historical fact, exactly the airspace-authorized shape the spec says gets no field: 'A parameter is not a rule, so it gets no entry at all.' If that were all the corpus deferred, definedElsewhere would be wrong. What saves it is the parenthetical: the rule uses the term 'depreciation adjustments', and the corpus fixes that term's MEANING in section 1250(b)(3), which is the spec's test ('its meaning is fixed in a corpus that was not admitted'). The term is load-bearing, not decorative: whether 'if applicable' applies at all turns on whether the taxpayer ever determined depreciation adjustments, and only 1250(b)(3) says what counts as one. It is a definition, not a rule the engine must run instead, so it is not a pointer to a different rule. Caveat the change does not address: the entry's note never says in the spec's own terms that the method itself is a caller-supplied parameter. The note's 'The rule is a constraint on the method rather than a method' gestures at it; the spec asks for a note 'saying the input comes from outside'. I would make that explicit, so a later reader does not think definedElsewhere is carrying the method.

verdicts.citation: the portion of the depreciation adjustments (as defined in section 1250(b)(3)) attributable to the property for periods after May 6, 1997
verdicts.reason: usc-26-1250 is right and consistent. manifest-references.json declares {sourceId: usc-26-1250, citation: § 1250(b)(3), admitted: false}, so it resolves to a manifest reference marked not admitted, which is what the spec and 0026 § 3 require. depreciation-not-excludable quotes the same statute for the same term in § 1.121-1(d) and carries the identical definedElsewhere {reference: usc-26-1250}. Two entries deferring the same term to the same unadmitted corpus by the same reference id is exactly the consistency wanted. Nothing here is wrong.

verdicts.citation: D may exclude $13,000 of the gain from the sale of her house because, under paragraph (e)(1) of this section, she is not required to allocate gain to the business use within the dwelling unit.
verdicts.reason: Three objections, in rising order of seriousness. (a) TABLE MECHANICS. Read strictly, row 2 -- 'status: mapped or blocked -- read, not built' -- matches this entry (status: mapped) and first match wins, so the table gives UnsupportedRule, not MissingRulesData. The table plainly INTENDS rows 3-8 to describe a built entry, but the row-2 wording swallows every mapped entry in this map, including depreciation-not-excludable and dwelling-unit-definition, whose notes also claim MissingRulesData. On the intended reading, row 3 (carries definedElsewhere) fires before row 6 (ambiguity.fate: unresolved), so MissingRulesData is the answer and RequiresInterpretation is unreachable. That is the ordering working as designed; the row-2 wording is a separate defect worth fixing. (b) ONE REASON CANNOT HONESTLY SERVE BOTH CASES. Case (a), depreciation WAS taken: the caller needs to know what counts as a depreciation adjustment to confirm 'if applicable' and to identify the method; MissingRulesData naming § 1250(b)(3) is honest and actionable -- go read that statute and you can proceed. Case (b), no depreciation ever taken and an allocation is nevertheless required: the caller is handed MissingRulesData pointing at § 1250(b)(3), reads all of § 1250(b)(3), and still has no method, because the missing thing is not in that statute -- it is not anywhere. The corpus states no method and names no decider. That is RequiresInterpretation in substance, and MissingRulesData sends the caller down a dead end while looking actionable. So no, one reason does not serve both, and row 3's precedence over row 6 makes the less honest of the two win in the case where honesty matters most. (c) THE NOTE CONTRADICTS THE RUNTIME ROW IT DEFENDS. The note says 'An engine can answer wherever depreciation was taken and must decline where none was.' But definedElsewhere fires unconditionally at row 3: the entry declines in BOTH cases. The note describes behaviour the entry as written cannot produce. WHAT I THINK SHOULD HAPPEN: the two defects are different and should be two entries or a split condition -- the depreciation-taken branch resolvable once § 1250(b)(3) is admitted, the no-depreciation branch genuinely unresolved and reachable by a ruling. Failing that, the note must stop claiming the engine can answer the first case, and must say in terms that a caller who obtains § 1250(b)(3) still gets no answer in the second.

verdicts.citation: No allocation is required if both the residential and non-residential portions of the property are within the same dwelling unit.
verdicts.reason: Two parts. (i) AS A CHANGE: nothing moves, because nothing changes. Every field is identical before and after; only the definedElsewhere key's position in the object differs, and JSON object key order carries no meaning. The note did NOT change -- it is byte-identical. So the brief's question ('the note changed -- read it and say whether it claims anything the corpus does not support') cannot be answered about a change. (ii) AS A STANDING CLAIM, and this is the real finding: the note and the ambiguity.question BOTH misread Example 6, and the corpus contradicts them. The question says the no-method gap is the case where 'no depreciation was ever taken -- (e)(4) Example 6 is exactly that case', and the note says the decline 'is the case Example 6 turns on'. Example 6 is not that case. In Example 6 the business use is WITHIN a single dwelling unit, so under (e)(1) no allocation is required at all and (e)(3) never fires -- the corpus says so in the example's own words, cited above. (e)(3) applies only where a portion is 'separate from the dwelling unit'. The genuine gap case is a SEPARATE portion on which no depreciation was ever taken, and the corpus gives no example of it -- Examples 1, 2 and 3 all involve separate portions on which depreciation WAS claimed ($9,000; $4,800 and $3,000; $2,000). The gap is real; the instance named for it is wrong. Structurally this is confirmed by the map itself: allocation-required is suspendedBy no-allocation-within-dwelling-unit, so an Example 6 fact pattern is already suspended upstream and never reaches this entry. Both sentences should be rewritten to state the gap without Example 6, or with the separate-portion-no-depreciation case named as the one the corpus does not illustrate.

Right in principle, though I cannot see it happen: neither half of diff.json has a crossReferences array, so nothing was removed in the file I was given. On the principle: the spec is explicit -- 'It answers the pointer, once. ... A crossReferences item for the same pointer answers it a second time, as prose, and check-map.py --only cross-references refuses it (#62).' 0026 § 4 says the same from the detection side: 'A pointer whose words name the entry's own definedElsewhere reference is claimed by that field, which 0020 § 4 made the only place it is answered.' The sole exception in 0026 § 4 is a scope: out entry quoted only to decline a section; this entry is scope: in and works a rule, so the exception does not reach it. I checked the evidence for other pointers that would need their own item: '(as defined in section 1250(b)(3))' is the only one in the quoted span. depreciation-not-excludable keeps a crossReferences item, but for a different pointer ('The section 121 exclusion' -> exclusion-of-gain), which is precisely the night-waiver-bar pattern the spec permits.

verdicts.citation: Example 6 Non-residential use within the dwelling unit, property not depreciated.The facts are the same as in Example 5, except that D is not entitled to claim any depreciation deductions with respect to her business use of the house.
verdicts.reason: Things the entry gets wrong or that the change should have touched and did not: (1) The Example 6 misreading in both the ambiguity.question and the note -- see question 4. This is the one substantive error I found in the entry, and it survives the change untouched. (2) The note's 'An engine can answer wherever depreciation was taken' is unreachable behaviour given row 3 -- see question 3(c). (3) The entry does not name dwelling-unit-definition in dependsOn, although (e)(3) allocates 'between the residential and the non-residential portions', and which portions are separate turns on the same term whose content sits in the unadmitted § 280A(f)(1). It reaches that term transitively through allocation-required, which is arguably enough under 0026 § 2's test, but dwelling-unit-definition's own note claims 'three entries depend on it' and I can see only one in the material given -- worth counting. (4) Example 6 says D 'is not entitled to claim' depreciation, which is not the same predicate as 'no depreciation was ever taken'; the note conflates entitlement with what was taken. § 1.121-1(d) speaks of 'depreciation adjustments ... attributable to the property', a third predicate again. If the no-depreciation branch is ever written as its own entry, which of these three the condition turns on has to be decided from § 1250(b)(3), not from the note. (5) Correspondence-table row 2's wording, above -- not this entry's fault, but it defeats the MissingRulesData claim of every mapped entry in this map if read as written.

1.limits: I judged only the seven files named. The before/after in diff.json are the same object, so I could not review the change the brief describes (removal of a crossReferences item, RequiresInterpretation -> MissingRulesData, a changed note); if that change exists, it is not in this file and my questions 3, 4 and 5 are answered against the entry's current text rather than against a transition. I did not read the map, the manifest, check-map.py, 0005, 0009, 0020, 0021, 0027, 0059, any issue or PR, or any decision above 0026, so where the note cites 0059 and 0027 I took the citation at face value and judged only whether the corpus supports the claim beside it. I did not read section 1250(b)(3) or section 280A(f)(1); my claim that § 1250(b)(3) cannot supply an allocation method where none was used rests on § 1.121-1(e)(3) making the method the TAXPAYER'S historical choice, not the statute's, which is on the face of the corpus. The count of entries depending on dwelling-unit-definition could not be checked from four sibling entries.

preliminary.finding: The rebuilt diff.json is the transition the brief describes and is materially different from round 1's file. before: unresolvedReason RequiresInterpretation, one crossReferences item for 'section 1250(b)(3)' with an unmapped reason, no definedElsewhere. after: definedElsewhere usc-26-1250, no crossReferences, unresolvedReason MissingRulesData, note extended by four sentences. Everything else -- id, name, locator, kind, scope, clarity, ambiguity.question, ambiguity.fate, dependsOn, evidence, status, enabledBy, and the note's first two sentences -- is byte-identical. My round-1 'semanticallyInert: true' was an artefact of the broken file and is withdrawn: see semanticallyInert below.

verdicts.citation: using the same method of allocation that the taxpayer used to determine depreciation adjustments (as defined in section 1250(b)(3)), if applicable.
verdicts.reason: Two halves. (i) DOES A READING MOVE? The entry's reading of the corpus does not move: evidence, scope, clarity, ambiguity.question and ambiguity.fate are unchanged, so what the entry claims § 1.121-1(e)(3) SAYS, and what it claims is open about it, are identical before and after. What moves is the answer the entry gives. Before, no row 3 match (no definedElsewhere), so the first substantive row that fires is row 6, ambiguity.fate: unresolved -> RequiresInterpretation, which is what the before declares. After, row 3 fires -> MissingRulesData, which is what the after declares. Both halves are internally consistent with correspondence-table.md; they simply land on different rows. So this is not a change of representation only. It is a change of declared runtime answer, made by adding a field that outranks the one that was deciding. That is a real change and it must be reviewed as one -- the round-1 file made it invisible. (ii) IS REMOVING THE CROSS-REFERENCE CORRECT? Yes, and it is not optional. defined-elsewhere-spec.md: 'It answers the pointer, once. ... A crossReferences item for the same pointer answers it a second time, as prose, and check-map.py --only cross-references refuses it (#62).' 0026 § 4 from the detection side: 'A pointer whose words name the entry's own definedElsewhere reference is claimed by that field, which 0020 § 4 made the only place it is answered.' The single exception in 0026 § 4 is a scope: out entry quoted only to decline a section; this entry is scope: in and works a rule, so the exception does not reach it. I re-checked the evidence span for any other pointer that would need an item of its own: '(as defined in section 1250(b)(3))' is the only one. So the after must have zero crossReferences, and it does. Removal is correct. depreciation-not-excludable keeps an item for a different pointer ('The section 121 exclusion' -> exclusion-of-gain), which is the permitted night-waiver-bar pattern.

verdicts.citation: The sentence above about answering wherever depreciation was taken is about what the rule permits once the term is supplied, not about what this entry returns: the entry declines unconditionally, by row 3, and an engine answers either case only on an owner's ruling.
verdicts.reason: HONEST, not papering over -- say it plainly. The appended sentence does not soften, qualify away, or re-describe the contradiction I raised; it states the fact I raised, in my terms, and names the mechanism: the entry declines unconditionally, by row 3. It draws the distinction that was missing (what the RULE permits vs. what the ENTRY returns) and it says where an answer could come from (an owner's ruling). If a reader reaches it, they cannot be misled. Papering over would be a sentence that made the original sound true; this one makes it false-as-read and says so. Nothing in the appended text claims anything the corpus contradicts: 'the corpus leaves a gap of its own where no depreciation applies' is on the face of (e)(3), which fixes a method only 'if applicable' and states no other; 'depreciation-not-excludable quotes the same statute for the same term and has always declared it this way' is verified against sibling-entries.json for the current state (definedElsewhere usc-26-1250, note claiming MissingRulesData) -- the 'has always' is a history claim I cannot check from these files and should not be in a note that is otherwise checkable; 'by row 3' is verified against correspondence-table.md. TWO RESERVATIONS, neither fatal. (a) DRAFTING. A note that needs its fourth sentence to unsay its second is worse than a note that says it once. The offending sentence is still there, in the engine's own vocabulary -- 'An engine can answer wherever depreciation was taken and must decline where none was' -- and a reader who stops at sentence two is misled about the entry's behaviour. Honesty is satisfied; clarity is not. The fix belongs in the sentence, not after it. It should read, roughly: 'The rule permits an answer wherever depreciation was taken and states no method where none was. This entry returns neither: it declines in both cases, because the term itself is not supplied.' That keeps the observation about the rule, drops the false claim about the engine, and makes the fourth sentence unnecessary. (b) CITING A ROW BY NUMBER. 'by row 3' pins the note to a positional index in a table that is edited; insert a row above it and the note silently becomes wrong. Name the field ('by its definedElsewhere') and it cannot rot.

verdicts.citation: the taxpayer must allocate the basis and the amount realized ... using the same method of allocation that the taxpayer used to determine depreciation adjustments (as defined in section 1250(b)(3)), if applicable.
verdicts.reason: THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT HOLDS. I attacked it and it survived, and the corpus gives it a better support than the author used. My round-1 objection assumed a caller who KNOWS they are in the no-depreciation branch, and asked what MissingRulesData does for them. That caller does not exist at call time. To be in the no-depreciation branch is to have determined no depreciation adjustments, and what counts as a depreciation adjustment is fixed by § 1250(b)(3) and nowhere in the admitted corpus. So an engine returning RequiresInterpretation would be asserting a branch it cannot establish -- a worse fault than returning the reason for the wall it can actually see. First-match-wins ordering, with row 3 above row 6, is doing exactly the right thing here, and it is the discipline, not an accident of row order. STRONGER THAN THE AUTHOR PUT IT, from the corpus's own face: Example 6 says D 'is not entitled to claim any depreciation deductions', which is a predicate about entitlement, not about what was taken or what was determined. A caller who knows no deductions were claimed still does not know that no depreciation adjustments were determined -- those are three different predicates and only § 1250(b)(3) relates them. That is the branch-indistinguishability claim, demonstrated without leaving the corpus. WHAT STILL STANDS, in weakened form. MissingRulesData is honest about the first wall and silent about the second. The reason promises, by its name and by every other use of it in this map, that supplying the named data lets the engine proceed. In the no-depreciation branch that promise is not kept: obtain § 1250(b)(3), learn the branch, and (e)(3) still names no method and no decider, because it makes the method the TAXPAYER'S historical choice. Nothing machine-readable records that. The author's mitigation -- 'the gap stays in the question, where a ruling under 0027 can reach it' -- is the right place for it and the ambiguity block does survive intact in the after, so the residual is recorded, just in prose. I accept that as sufficient. THE CASE THAT DEFEATS IT, and it is a dated expiry rather than a refutation: admit usc-26-1250. The day the statute is admitted, definedElsewhere cannot stand (0026 § 3: check-map.py refuses a reference marked admitted: true), row 3 stops firing, row 6 fires, and this entry returns RequiresInterpretation -- for the no-depreciation branch, correctly, and for the depreciation-taken branch, wrongly, where the rule is by then fully determinate. The 'first wall is the first wall in both' argument is true only while the two branches are indistinguishable, and admission is exactly what distinguishes them. So the counter-argument is sound and time-limited, and the entry carries no record of what admission obliges. Recommendation, not a blocker: one clause in the note saying that if § 1250(b)(3) is ever admitted this entry must split, the depreciation-taken branch becoming resolvable and only the no-depreciation branch staying unresolved.

verdicts.citation: D may exclude $13,000 of the gain from the sale of her house because, under paragraph (e)(1) of this section, she is not required to allocate gain to the business use within the dwelling unit.
verdicts.reason: CONFIRMED from diff.json: ambiguity.question is byte-identical before and after and still reads '(e)(4) Example 6 is exactly that case'; the note's first two sentences are carried over verbatim, including 'it is the case Example 6 turns on'. Neither is corrected. Filing the misreading as a separate defect is legitimate scope discipline and I would not block a change for leaving an inherited error alone. That is not what happened. This change does not leave the error alone -- it BUILDS ON IT. The appended sentence 'the corpus leaves a gap of its own where no depreciation applies' is now the load-bearing justification for keeping the ambiguity block at all and for the whole first-wall argument, and the only instance the entry offers for that gap is Example 6, which is not an instance of it. Example 6's business use is within a single dwelling unit, so under (e)(1) no allocation is required, (e)(3) never fires, and the map confirms it structurally: allocation-required is suspendedBy no-allocation-within-dwelling-unit, so an Example 6 fact pattern is suspended upstream and never reaches this entry. The real gap case is a SEPARATE portion on which no depreciation was taken, and the corpus illustrates it nowhere -- Examples 1, 2 and 3 all involve separate portions on which depreciation WAS claimed ($9,000; $4,800 and $3,000; $2,000). So the change adds new text resting on a citation it knows to be wrong, without a hedge. It also introduces a FOURTH phrasing of the predicate -- 'where no depreciation applies' -- beside 'no depreciation was ever taken' (question), 'is not entitled to claim' (Example 6) and 'depreciation adjustments ... attributable to the property' (§ 1.121-1(d)); these are not the same test, and which one governs can only be settled from § 1250(b)(3). NOT GROUNDS TO REJECT the change: the gap it asserts is real on the face of (e)(3) and does not depend on Example 6 being an instance of it. But the change is conditionally correct -- it is correct only if the separately filed defect is actually fixed. Were that fix dropped, this change would have deepened the error rather than being neutral to it. A single clause would have cost nothing: name the gap without Example 6, or mark the instance as under separate review.

verdicts.citation: Rows are checked in order and the first match wins. Not-in-scope and not-built dominate; the rest describe what a *built* entry returns.
verdicts.reason: NEITHER a defect in the change nor, materially, in the table. My round-1 objection is resolved by the table's own text, which I under-read. Row 2's cell is 'status: mapped or blocked -- read, not built', and the preamble says not-built dominates while 'the rest describe what a built entry returns'. That marks row 2 as a PIPELINE-STAGE gate, not a substantive classification on a par with rows 1 and 3: it says this entry has been read into the map and no engine code exists for it yet, and a later stage turns it. Read that way, the MissingRulesData claims in this entry and in its siblings are claims about what the built entry will return, and they do not collide with row 2 at all. My round-1 reading -- that row 2 swallows every mapped entry in the map -- treated a stage gate as a field test, which the preamble forecloses. NOT the change's fault and not worth a change here. One clarity nit, offered and no more: the column header is 'A map entry that is...', which invites reading 'status: mapped' as a field predicate like 'carries definedElsewhere'; a reader who scans the grid without the preamble makes my error. Four words in the cell ('until a later stage builds it') would close it. ONE CONSEQUENCE WORTH STATING, because it bears on how this change can be verified: if row 2 governs today, then rows 3-8 are counterfactual for every entry in this map, and no test that runs today can distinguish this change's before from its after. The transition is real but currently unobservable, so it can only be reviewed by reading, which is what this review is.

verdicts.citation: It is answered here rather than by `definedElsewhere` because this entry already carries an `ambiguity` block and the schema excludes the two on one entry; the report records that as finding 4.
verdicts.reason: Things the real diff reveals that round 1 could not see. (1) THE DELETED REASON ASSERTED A SCHEMA CONSTRAINT THE CHANGE ITSELF VIOLATES, and nobody says which of the two is wrong. The before's unmapped prose, cited above, states that the schema excludes ambiguity and definedElsewhere on one entry. The after carries BOTH. So either that claim was false when written, or the schema has since changed, or the after is schema-invalid. Nothing in the change records which. defined-elsewhere-spec.md states no such exclusion -- if anything it points the other way, noting that hazardous-material and civil-twilight-alaska 'both previously carried the reason in an ambiguity block, on entries that are not ambiguous', which reads as a complaint about misplacement, not a prohibition on co-occurrence. And no sibling in sibling-entries.json carries an ambiguity block at all, so the after is the only instance of the combination in the material I was given and I cannot verify it passes. THIS IS THE ONE HARD ACTION ITEM OF THIS REVIEW: run check-map.py against the after and confirm ambiguity + definedElsewhere on a single entry is accepted. If it is, the deleted sentence was false and the change is silently correcting a false claim -- which should be said out loud, because that false claim is the stated reason the pointer was answered as prose in the first place, i.e. the whole premise of the before. (2) PROVENANCE DELETED. The removed item was the only place in the entry naming 'finding 4' of the report. The note's replacement ('Both facts are recorded since 0059') cites a different artefact and does not carry the finding forward. Deleting a field is the right call; dropping the only pointer to the finding that produced it is a small loss that one clause would fix. (3) AN unresolvedReason THAT NO LONGER ANSWERS ITS OWN BLOCK. In the after, ambiguity.question describes an interpretive gap ('the corpus states no other and names nobody to choose one') while ambiguity.unresolvedReason says MissingRulesData. The field now records the runtime row rather than why THIS ambiguity is unresolved. That is defensible given the table's vocabulary is the kernel's, and the author's 'the gap stays in the question' is an accurate description of where it went -- but the consequence is that nothing machine-readable in this map now says an interpretive gap exists here. Before the change, one field did. That is a genuine loss of signal and it is the honest residue of my round-1 question-3 objection; it is the thing a future reader is most likely to miss. (4) MY ROUND-1 dependsOn POINT IS UNTOUCHED and unverifiable from these files: dwelling-unit-definition's note still claims 'three entries depend on it' and I can still see exactly one (allocation-required). This entry reaches the term only transitively. Worth counting against the full map, outside this review's boundary. (5) NOT INERT. Round 1 reported semanticallyInert: true against an identical before/after. Against the real diff that answer is false and I withdraw it.

2.limits: I judged only the eight files named, and wrote only into this directory. I did not read the map, the manifest, check-map.py, the schema, 0005, 0009, 0020, 0021, 0027, 0059, any issue, any PR, or any decision above 0026; where the note cites 0059 and 0027 I took the citation at face value and judged only whether the corpus supports the claim beside it. I did not read section 1250(b)(3) or section 280A(f)(1). My claim that § 1250(b)(3) cannot supply an allocation method where none was used rests on § 1.121-1(e)(3) making the method the TAXPAYER'S historical choice, which is on the face of the corpus. My claim that the three depreciation predicates (entitled to claim / taken / adjustments determined) can come apart rests on their being different words in the corpus, not on the statute. The schema question in verdict 6(1) is the one finding I cannot settle from these files and it needs check-map.py run against the after. The correspondence table I was given is 33 lines and ends mid-sentence inside the row-8 discussion; my reading of row 2 rests on the preamble and the row cell, both of which are present in full.
